meta.title: The XMSG protocol catalog
meta.what_this_is: The master list. Every protocol registry in this folder is named here, in the order a reader should meet them. Tools read THIS to find the registries - nothing has a hard-coded list, so adding a registry means adding it here and nowhere else.
meta.the_rule: A registry file that is not in this catalog, or a catalog entry with no file, FAILS THE BUILD. That is what stops a new protocol being documented and then quietly forgotten, or a deleted one lingering in the docs.
how_it_is_checked: RegistryCatalogTests - every file listed exists, every .json in the folder is listed, and nothing is described twice
RegistryEnumCompletenessTests - every C# enum a registry binds is described in FULL, and the registry describes nothing the enum no longer has
ProtocolRegistryConformanceTests - the values, offsets and masks match the code
generate.py --check - the generated markdown is not stale

status_values.MEASURED: Observed on the wire or carved from the kernel, with the evidence named.
status_values.INFERRED: Follows from something measured, or read from the ND manuals, but not itself observed here.
status_values.UNKNOWN: We copy it, mirror it, or leave it alone. NOT safe to compute or vary.
status_values.SUPERSEDED: A reading that was believed and is now disproved. Kept so it is not re-derived.

registries.title: The SINTRAN envelope
registries.one_line: the envelope every message rides in - the 7-word header, the bitfields, the ND link underneath
registries.read_first_because: every other registry assumes this header

registries.title: TAD - terminal sessions
registries.one_line: how a terminal on one machine reaches another: CONNECT-TO, the accept, then keystrokes and screen output

registries.title: FA - remote files, and the QFORM encoding
registries.one_line: open, read, write, create and list files on another machine - and the tag encoding its bodies use

registries.title: XROUT - names, routes and seats
registries.one_line: the phone book: it turns a registered name into an address, forwards the first letter, and counts the seats

registries.title: CHAT - rooms, members and what they say
registries.one_line: the one protocol Norsk Data never shipped: joining a room, saying something, and the two ports that decide who spends a seat
registries.read_first_because: it is the only registry here whose vocabulary we invented, so it is the one where a new message kind is declared before it is built

not_registries.note: Files in this folder that are NOT protocol registries, so the catalog check knows to ignore them.

consumers.note: Who reads these registries. Listed because it decides what the registries must CARRY - detail that is missing when a consumer is written has to be re-derived, which is the whole thing this folder exists to prevent.

planned.name: generated C# - PROVED as a dry run
planned.status: the generator exists and its output compiles clean
planned.what_was_proved: generate_csharp.py emits 11 files - enums with the plain-English meaning, the status and the evidence as XML doc comments, plus accessors for the header - and they build with GenerateDocumentationFile on and ZERO warnings.
planned.why_csharp_first: there is a hand-written C# library to compare against, so a shortfall shows up as a difference from working code rather than as a bug found later in a language nobody has tested. What the registry lacks for C# it would lack for C too.
planned.not_yet: it writes to a temp folder. Nothing under SRC is generated, and the hand-written library is still the one that runs.

planned.name: an XMSG protocol library in C
planned.status: FEASIBILITY PROVED - generator exists, output compiles and decodes real bytes
planned.why_it_is_recorded_here: so the registries keep what it will need instead of being trimmed to what C# happens to use
requires: an explicit width_bits and c_type on EVERY structure field - not implied by a word number
a c.struct name per structure, and a c.enum name plus prefix and underlying_type per enum block
byte order stated per structure - it is big-endian on the wire, and a C host is usually not
the plain-English meaning, which becomes the generated comment
planned.guarded_by: RegistryIsCodeGenerationReadyTests - the requirements above are checked, so the door cannot quietly close
planned.what_was_proved: generate_c.py emits four headers with no gaps. They compile under gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic, and a test program decodes a REAL captured D100 accept correctly: dest 102, source 100, Flags1 0x0021, checksum 0xD9F3. The XSDMC/XSDSY alias compares equal, and XFHIP/XFRRO both come out 0x2000.
planned.what_c_found_that_csharp_could_not: the snake-case helper split every capital, so the all-caps ND symbol XSLET became X_S_L_E_T. C# never saw it because it keeps member names verbatim. A second language is what tests the generator, not just the registry.
planned.not_yet: writes to a temp folder; no C library is built from it yet.

planned.name: TypeScript
planned.note: The bindings are keyed by language for this reason: adding typescript is a new key beside c, not a restructure. TypeScript needs no fixed-width types but does need the width and byte order to drive a DataView, which the registry already carries.

consumers.rule: Language-specific naming lives under bindings.<language>. Everything a generator needs that is NOT language-specific - width, byte order, meaning, status, evidence - lives on the field itself, so a new language costs one key and no re-authoring. Generating a SECOND language is what tests the generator itself - C demanded fixed widths, byte order and a flat namespace, and caught a naming bug C# could not.
